narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly more likely than passing, but it crosses the line used for admission, so the decision was unfavorable.

The strongest factor in your file was your third-year class standing. At the 5th decile, compared with an average near 6th among accepted students, this was the most influential factor and actually worked in your favor, slightly reducing the predicted risk of failure. However, two other factors outweighed it. Your LSAT score of 23 is far below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it was the second most important factor, pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.30, compared with an accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor and also pushed toward failure. Together, these academic indicators suggest that the model sees meaningful risk despite your third-year standing.

To improve your chances, focus on retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, since that is the clearest controllable weakness. If possible, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. Ask admissions for feedback, gain legal or paralegal experience, and consider reapplying when your LSAT and GPA profile are stronger. A lower-risk application would make the predicted probability of bar success more convincing.
